snippet.title: Suvendu Adhikari's New Bengal? 60 Days That Changed Everything
snippet.description:
West Bengal's political landscape has long been shaped by Mamata Banerjee and the Trinamool Congress. But what would happen if Suvendu Adhikari took charge and implemented a completely different governance model? In this video, we explore the idea of a "New Bengal" and examine the major cultural, political, and welfare changes that supporters believe could redefine the state's future. From education policies and administrative reforms to welfare schemes and Centre-State relations, we break down the key developments and their potential impact on Bengal's social and political landscape.
We also analyze how these changes could affect governance, public welfare, identity politics, and the broader debate over Bengal's future direction. Is this the beginning of a new political era, or simply a different vision for the state? Watch till the end for a detailed breakdown of the arguments, policies, and controversies surrounding the concept of a "New Bengal." If you enjoy factual explainers on politics, governance, public policy, and current affairs, don't forget to Like, Share, and Subscribe to Layered.

snippet.description:
When Iran threatened to disrupt the Strait of Hormuz, global energy markets reacted with concern. Yet India, one of the world's largest energy importers, managed the situation without major disruption. Why?
In this video, we break down India's multi-source energy strategy, its diplomatic engagement with key regional players, the role of the Indian Navy, and the vulnerabilities that still remain in India's energy and shipping ecosystem.
Discover how diversification, strategic planning, and diplomacy helped India navigate one of the most important energy-security challenges in recent years.

snippet.title: Policy-Making Process Explained | How Governments Create Policies
snippet.description:
The policy-making process explains how governments identify public problems, compare solutions, make decisions, implement policies, and evaluate results.

This process is often described as the policy cycle.

In this video, we explain the main stages of policymaking, who influences government decisions, why implementation matters, and why some policies fail.

What You’ll Learn
• how governments identify public problems
• how policy options are developed
• who influences policy decisions
• how policies are implemented
• why evaluation and improvement matter

Stage 1: Identifying the Problem
The process begins when an issue is recognised as a public problem.
Examples include:
• rising unemployment
• housing shortages
• traffic congestion
• poor healthcare access
• environmental pollution
• increasing crime
• weak education results
Not every problem receives government attention.
Political pressure, media coverage, public opinion, emergencies, and available resources can determine which issues become priorities.

Stage 2: Setting the Agenda
Agenda setting means deciding which problems government should focus on.
Politicians, civil servants, journalists, experts, businesses, and citizens may all influence this stage.
A problem may reach the government agenda because:
• the public demands action
• the media highlights it
• an emergency occurs
• research reveals serious risks
• political leaders make it a priority
If a problem does not reach the agenda, government action may never begin.

Stage 3: Developing Policy Options
Once the problem is recognised, policymakers study possible solutions.
They may consider:
• new laws
• financial support
• taxes or penalties
• public programmes
• regulations
• awareness campaigns
• partnerships with businesses
• no government action
Each option must be compared based on cost, fairness, political support, practicality, and expected results.

Stage 4: Policy Adoption
Policy adoption happens when the government officially chooses an option.
The decision may require:
• approval from parliament
• a ministerial decision
• new regulations
• budget approval
• support from local authorities
• agreement between departments

A policy may be technically strong but still fail to gain approval because of political disagreement or financial limits.

Stage 5: Implementation
Implementation is where the policy is turned into action.
This may require:
• funding
• trained employees
• government departments
• clear procedures
• technology
• public communication
• cooperation between organisations
This stage is often more difficult than creating the policy.
A good policy can fail if the organisation responsible for delivering it lacks money, staff, leadership, or planning.

Simple Example
Imagine the government wants to reduce air pollution.
The process may involve:
• identifying dangerous pollution levels
• placing the issue on the government agenda
• comparing transport and environmental policies
• approving stricter emissions rules
• enforcing the rules through public agencies
• measuring whether pollution falls
The government may then change the policy if the results are weak.

Stage 6: Policy Evaluation
Evaluation measures whether the policy achieved its goals.
Governments may examine:
• costs
• public satisfaction
• service quality
• social impact
• economic effects
• unexpected consequences
• whether the original problem improved
Evaluation is essential because a policy can appear successful politically while producing poor results in reality.

Stage 7: Policy Change or Termination
After evaluation, the government may:
• continue the policy
• improve it
• increase funding
• reduce its scale
• replace it
• end it completely
Policies should not continue forever simply because they already exist.
If a policy is ineffective, wasteful, or unfair, it should be changed.

Who Influences the Process?
The policy-making process may involve:
• elected politicians
• civil servants
• government departments
• experts and researchers
• courts
• businesses
• pressure groups
• media organisations
• citizens
This means public policy is shaped by both formal government institutions and outside influence.

Why Policies Fail
Policies may fail because of:
• poor problem definition
• weak evidence
• unrealistic goals
• insufficient funding
• political conflict
• poor communication
• weak implementation
• lack of evaluation
• public resistance
A policy can fail at any stage of the process.
That is why each stage must connect properly with the next.

Because at the end:
The policy-making process connects public problems with government decisions, practical action, and measurable results.

snippet.title: OTC Asia 2026: Energy security, LNG and AI in Asia Pacific, with Samuel Low
snippet.description:
Recorded at OTC Asia 2026 in Kuala Lumpur, Noah Brenner speaks with Samuel Low, Head of Advisory, Asia Pacific at Rystad Energy, about the forces shaping energy decision-making across the region.

The conversation explores what clients are asking around strategy, M&A and transaction support, gas and LNG market dynamics, strategic partnerships, the growing role of AI in advisory work, and why energy security remains high on the agenda across Asia Pacific.

In this interview:
+ Why LNG pricing and demand elasticity matter more than ever
+ How AI is improving speed, modeling and decision support
+ Why energy security is reshaping long-term priorities in the region

Trace the history of sumo, and explore how the sport was designed and modified to reflect ancient Japan’s culture and traditions.

--

Sumo wrestling is known across the world as a beloved form of entertainment, a grand display of strength, and an ode to Japan's ancient past and traditions. But surprisingly, many of these so-called "ancient" traditions were actually recent inventions. So, what were these fabricated practices, and how do they relate to sumo’s true history? Lee Thompson traces the evolution of the sport.

Lesson by Lee Thompson, directed by Masayoshi Nakamura, Good General.

snippet.title: Creating Lasting Change in Teams | Connected Leadership with Peter Boyd
snippet.description:
Once your team has its four Ps in place, the question becomes how to keep the bigger picture alive and hold each other accountable. This lesson lays out simple shared tools that let any team co-create and continuously refresh their work on one page.

Key topics:
- Holding each other accountable on progress
- Shared spreadsheets and slides as living team tools
- Connecting individual tabs to team goals
- Building the team's work on one page
- Walking through the connected strategy pyramid
- Revisiting documents at a cadence that works

📚 About the Course:

This course is designed to maximize your ability to create change at the individual, team and system levels. Through study, reflection, and deploying practical tools, you will establish a firm connection between your clearly articulated Purpose, effective Priorities, visualized Potential for success, and pathway to maximized Progress. But, what does that mean in practice?

When you take this course, you will:

Improve your ability to get the most out of life: Learn a simple practice to reflect on your purpose, clarify priorities, visualize your potential, and maximize your effectiveness at progressing towards your goals.

Strengthen your leadership toolkit: Tap into your unique leadership style and strengths and join or create a community of others to maximize your potential as a team.

Create change through systems thinking: Become a more effective agent of positive change and appreciate the power and complexity of system thinking.

Course Takeaways:
Improve your ability to get the most out of life
Strengthen your leadership toolkit
Practice and apply systems thinking to plan for change

snippet.title: Psychedelics, mind control, radiation-eating: The secret superpowers of fungi - Max G. Levy
snippet.description:
Dig into the vast and wild world of fungi, and explore how these organisms evolved to play a range of essential ecological roles.

--

The diverse fungal kingdom, which includes everything from baker’s yeast to edible mushrooms to foot infections, has long defied assumptions. Scientists estimate that somewhere between 2 and 12 million species of fungi remain undiscovered— either because they’re microscopic, live hidden within other species, or for other unknown reasons. Max G. Levy digs into the vast and wild world of fungi.

Lesson by Max G. Levy, directed by Petya Zlateva, Compote Collective.

snippet.title: 51 Years of Emergency: What Really Happened on 25 June 1975?
snippet.description:
On 25 June 1975, India entered one of the most controversial periods in its democratic history when the Emergency was declared under Article 352. Civil liberties were suspended, press censorship was imposed, and thousands of opposition leaders were detained. The move followed the Allahabad High Court's verdict against then Prime Minister Indira Gandhi, making the Emergency a defining moment in Indian politics.
In this video, we explain the reasons behind the Emergency, what happened during those 21 months, its impact on Indian democracy, and why it continues to shape political debates even after 51 years.

Explore the science of silica gel, and find out why these packets are everywhere and if they're actually dangerous to ingest.

This tiny packet pops up in packaging for everything — from TVs and guitar cases to sunscreen and snack foods. So why is silica gel everywhere, and what would actually happen if you ate it? snippet.title: Civil Service Explained | How Government Employees Work
snippet.description:
The civil service is the permanent administrative workforce of government.

Civil servants help implement public policies, manage departments, advise ministers, and deliver services such as taxation, education, healthcare, and public safety.

What You’ll Learn
• what the civil service means
• what civil servants do
• why political neutrality matters

What Is the Civil Service?
The civil service includes permanent government employees who work in ministries, departments, and public agencies.

They help governments:
• implement laws and policies
• manage public programmes
• deliver services to citizens

Who Are Civil Servants?
Civil servants may include:
• policy advisers
• administrators
• inspectors and programme officers

They are usually appointed based on qualifications, examinations, or professional experience.

Main Responsibilities
Civil servants are responsible for:
• advising government ministers
• managing budgets and records
• delivering public services

They turn political decisions into practical action.
Political Neutrality
Civil servants are expected to serve whichever elected government is in power.

They should:
• avoid political favouritism
• give professional advice
• apply rules fairly

This helps maintain continuity when governments change.

Simple Example
Imagine a government announces a new education policy.
Civil servants must:
• prepare the budget
• create procedures
• coordinate schools and teachers

The minister announces the policy.
The civil service helps make it work.

Why the Civil Service Matters
The civil service provides:
• continuity
• professional expertise
• administrative stability

Without it, government operations could stop whenever political leadership changes.

Common Problems
Civil services may face:
• slow decision-making
• political interference
• excessive bureaucracy

Poor recruitment or weak accountability can reduce performance.

Reality Check
Civil servants are often criticised when government services fail.
But many failures are also caused by weak policies, political pressure, or insufficient funding.

The brutal truth is:
A government cannot deliver strong public services without a competent and accountable civil service.

Why This Matters
Understanding the civil service explains:
• who implements government policy
• why governments continue after elections
• why professional administration matters

Because at the end:
Politicians set direction, but civil servants keep the machinery of government running.

snippet.title: Evolution of Information Systems | Mainframes, Internet, Cloud and AI
snippet.description:
Modern organisations use cloud platforms, databases, mobile applications, and artificial intelligence.

But Information Systems did not begin with modern computers.

They developed gradually as businesses searched for better ways to store information, automate work, and make decisions.

Here’s the reality:

The history of Information Systems is the story of how organisations moved from manual records to intelligent, connected, and data-driven systems.

In this lecture, we explore the history and evolution of Information Systems, from early paper-based methods to modern AI-powered platforms.

What You’ll Learn
• how organisations managed information before computers
• why early computers were introduced into businesses
• how mainframes changed data processing
• how personal computers transformed office work
• how the internet connected organisations globally
• how cloud computing and AI changed modern Information Systems

Early Manual Systems
Before computers, organisations depended on:
• paper records
• handwritten ledgers
• filing cabinets
• printed reports
• manual calculations
• face-to-face communication

These systems worked for smaller organisations.

But as businesses grew, manual systems became slow, expensive, and difficult to manage.

The Mainframe Era
During the 1950s and 1960s, large organisations began using mainframe computers.

These machines were expensive and mainly used for:
• payroll processing
• accounting
• inventory records
• government data
• large calculations

At this stage, Information Systems focused mainly on automating routine transactions.

The Management Information Systems Era

During the 1960s and 1970s, organisations began using computer-generated reports to support managers.

This led to the development of Management Information Systems, also known as MIS.

MIS helped managers monitor:
• sales
• costs
• production
• employee performance
• inventory levels

Information was no longer used only for record-keeping.

It was also used for management and control.

The Personal Computer Era
During the 1980s, personal computers became more affordable.
Employees could now use:
• spreadsheets
• word-processing software
• desktop databases
• presentation tools
• business applications

Computing moved from specialised departments to ordinary offices.

The Internet Era
During the 1990s, the internet transformed Information Systems.
Businesses could now connect with:
• customers
• suppliers
• employees
• international markets
• online services

This period introduced:
• e-commerce
• company websites
• email communication
• online banking
• digital supply chains

The Enterprise Systems Era
Large organisations began integrating departments through systems such as:
• Enterprise Resource Planning
• Customer Relationship Management
• Supply Chain Management
• Human Resource Information Systems

Instead of each department using separate information, enterprise systems created a more connected organisation.

The Cloud and Mobile Era
Cloud computing allowed organisations to access software and data through the internet.

• inventory levels

Information was no longer used only for record-keeping.

• spreadsheets
• word-processing software
• desktop databases
• presentation tools
• business applications

Computing moved from specialised departments to ordinary offices.

snippet.description:
When a powerful earthquake struck Venezuela, India responded within hours with Operation Amistad. But this mission is about much more than sending relief supplies. India deployed emergency medical teams, field hospitals, life-saving medicines, and the innovative BHISHM Cube—a modular emergency medical system capable of establishing critical healthcare facilities in disaster-hit regions within hours.
Operation Amistad highlights India's growing ability to act as a global first responder. Following missions like Operation Dost in Turkey and Operation Brahma in Myanmar, India is steadily building a reputation as a nation that delivers rapid-response capabilities, not just financial aid. This mission also showcases India's rising humanitarian diplomacy and the global potential of Made-in-India technologies.
In this video, we explain how Operation Amistad works, what makes the BHISHM Cube special, and why India's role in global disaster relief is becoming increasingly important.

snippet.title: Accountability and Transparency in Government Explained
snippet.description:
Accountability and transparency are essential parts of good governance.

In this video, we explain how public officials are held responsible, why government information should be accessible, and how both reduce corruption and improve public trust.

What You’ll Learn
• what accountability means
• what transparency means
• why both are essential

What Is Accountability?
Accountability means public officials must explain and justify their actions.

They may be held responsible by:
• citizens and elected bodies
• courts and auditors
• regulators and the media

Officials should face consequences when they misuse power or public money.

What Is Transparency?
Transparency means government decisions and information are open to the public.

This may include:
• public budgets
• contracts and policies
• performance reports

Transparency helps citizens understand how government operates.

Main Difference
The simplest difference is:
Transparency makes information visible.
Accountability makes decision-makers responsible.
Transparency supports accountability, but information alone is not enough without action.

Simple Example
Imagine a government department spends millions on a public project.
Transparency means the budget, contract, and spending records are publicly available.
Accountability means officials must explain delays, waste, or misuse of funds.

Why They Matter
Accountability and transparency can:
• reduce corruption
• improve public trust
• strengthen public services

They also encourage officials to make more careful decisions.
Common Problems
These principles may fail because of:
• hidden information
• weak investigations
• political interference

Publishing information is useless if it is incomplete, confusing, or ignored.

Tools for Accountability
Governments may use:
• independent audits
• parliamentary oversight
• complaint and appeal systems

Freedom of information laws can also help citizens access public records.

Reality Check
Governments often claim to be transparent simply because they publish reports.

But information that is late, incomplete, or impossible to understand is not real transparency.

The brutal truth is:
Transparency without consequences is just visibility, not accountability.

Why This Matters
Understanding these ideas explains:
• how officials are monitored
• why public records matter
• how citizens can challenge decisions

Because at the end:
Good government requires both open information and real responsibility.

localized.title: Accountability and Transparency in Government Explained
localized.description:
Accountability and transparency are essential parts of good governance.

In this video, we explain how public officials are held responsible, why government information should be accessible, and how both reduce corruption and improve public trust.

What You’ll Learn
• what accountability means
• what transparency means
• why both are essential

What Is Accountability?
Accountability means public officials must explain and justify their actions.

They may be held responsible by:
• citizens and elected bodies
• courts and auditors
• regulators and the media

Officials should face consequences when they misuse power or public money.

What Is Transparency?
Transparency means government decisions and information are open to the public.

This may include:
• public budgets
• contracts and policies
• performance reports

Transparency helps citizens understand how government operates.

Main Difference
The simplest difference is:
Transparency makes information visible.
Accountability makes decision-makers responsible.
Transparency supports accountability, but information alone is not enough without action.

Simple Example
Imagine a government department spends millions on a public project.
Transparency means the budget, contract, and spending records are publicly available.
Accountability means officials must explain delays, waste, or misuse of funds.

Why They Matter
Accountability and transparency can:
• reduce corruption
• improve public trust
• strengthen public services

They also encourage officials to make more careful decisions.
Common Problems
These principles may fail because of:
• hidden information
• weak investigations
• political interference

Publishing information is useless if it is incomplete, confusing, or ignored.

Tools for Accountability
Governments may use:
• independent audits
• parliamentary oversight
• complaint and appeal systems

Freedom of information laws can also help citizens access public records.

Reality Check
Governments often claim to be transparent simply because they publish reports.

But information that is late, incomplete, or impossible to understand is not real transparency.

The brutal truth is:
Transparency without consequences is just visibility, not accountability.

Why This Matters
Understanding these ideas explains:
• how officials are monitored
• why public records matter
• how citizens can challenge decisions

Because at the end:
Good government requires both open information and real responsibility.

snippet.title: Roman Roads: The Engineering Masterpiece That Changed Civilization
snippet.description:
Roman roads were built 2,000 years ago. Some are still in use today. Modern asphalt lasts 15 years. 

So what did Rome know that we forgot?

This isn't just construction history, it's a masterclass in engineering that no civilization has matched since.

The Roman road system stretched over 250,000 miles (400,000 km), enough to circle the Earth 10 times. Every road was built to a military-grade standard: layered with crushed stone, volcanic aggregate, and interlocking rock that flexed under pressure instead of cracking. No concrete. No machines. No GPS. Just geometry, logistics, and Roman discipline.
